instagram.caption:
Every dentist promises "quality care". So nobody remembers any of them.

A good tagline answers the real reason people hold back. For nervous patients that's the pain, not the quality. Then run the swap test: put your line under a competitor's logo. If it still works, it was never your line.

The rule: answer the real reason. If a rival could say it, it isn't yours.

Practise it on a real brief: play Copywriter Chronicles free at workexp.org (link in bio).

instagram.caption:
"October newsletter" goes in the bin. "Does your radiator have a cold patch at the top?" gets read.

An email has two jobs before anything else. The subject line earns the open. The first line earns the next ten seconds. A question the reader can check for themselves beats any discount.

The rule: give them something to check, then keep the promise in line one.

A poster gets a few seconds from someone who's already walking past.

Give them a paragraph and they glance, find nothing to hold on to, and keep walking. Give the eye a path instead: one line grabs, one explains, one tells you what to do. Then squint at it. If line one survives, it works.

The rule: one grabs, one explains, one tells them what to do.

instagram.caption:
Somebody wrote this notification. The phone finished it for them.

Every format has a space budget: a billboard, a lock screen, a button. Go over it and something gets cut, usually from the end, usually the part that mattered. So cut your own words first. Really, very, we think, also: the fillers go.

The rule: write to the space. If it doesn't fit, it isn't finished.

instagram.caption:
Nobody can write down a web address at 60 miles an hour.

On a page, the eye can go back. On air, every word goes past once. So pick one idea, say the name more than once, and give every line one breath. One sound. One idea. "Hartley's. Bread that crackles."

The rule: one idea, said more than once. Every line in one breath.

instagram.caption:
"Learn more" is a dead end pretending to be a next step.

By the time someone reaches your button, they're interested. What stops them is a worry, usually two. A good call to action has three parts: a verb, what they get, and an answer to the worry. "Book a free first climb. Beginners' session, no membership needed."

The rule: name the action, then answer the two worries.

instagram.caption:
"Get in touch for pricing" quietly loses customers every day.

When you hide a number, people don't leave it blank. They fill it in themselves, and they guess high. Every product has a short list of things people are nervous to ask, and price is almost always first. Say it plainly, and say it first.

The rule: say the worrying thing first. A real answer beats an imagined one.

instagram.caption:
These four ads come from the same company. You would never know.

People meet ads one at a time, weeks apart. If they don't sound related, nothing adds up. A brand's voice is the set of choices that don't change: the words, the rhythm, the look. Then the message can change. A teaser that makes people curious, a launch that pays it off.

The rule: keep the voice, change the message.

instagram.caption:
Two hours before launch, legal rejects your headline. Now what?

Most claims that fall apart were sitting on top of a true one. So dig, until you hit something you can prove. "100% natural" becomes "Just pressed apples. Nothing added." And ask for time: an extra hour is cheap, a weak line on a billboard for six weeks isn't.

The rule: dig for the true claim, and ask for the time to find it.
